To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the smart city benchmarking process should: (a) take into consideration the different perspectives and the different levels of aggregation of data, (b) be grounded on the traces of people, (c) be based on the territorial "state of flow".

(a) the current approaches to smart city benchmarking do not take into account the "people centredness" of smart cities and (b) a novel definition of the "smart city", based on the territorial flow, is proposed and, as a result, a novel path towards smart city benchmarking emerges.

(a) smart cities are a complex system and the city rankings are a partial view of this system, (b) the smart city is not an objective reality, but rather a subjective perception, and (c) a smart city is a state of flow, a dynamic equilibrium of the system that can be measured and compared.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the following research questions: (1) What is the state of the art of smart city benchmarking? (2) How can smart city analytics be redefined in order to be more effective? (3) What is a smart city? (4) What are the main challenges and opportunities for future research in smart city benchmarking?
the following questions: (1) How can smart city rankings be improved? (2) How can smart cities analytics be redesigned?
the need for new approaches to city benchmark, which should be based on a more inclusive vision, able to take into account both the "hard data" and the people perspective.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
, in the current context, a smart city can be defined as a city where a state of flow is reached, in which people are the centre and the main drivers of the smart city evolution.
smart cities are not a mere aggregation of technologies but a complex system where the role of people is fundamental.
smart cities are the ones where people can live, work, learn, and enjoy life in a sustainable and resilient environment.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the "Smart City Analytics" needs to be redefined in order to take into account the "people centred vision" and the "territorial state of flow".
the future smart city is not only about data, but it is about people and their needs, expectations and aspirations.

, by means of a critical analysis of current smart cities benchmarking, we propose the need for the integration of bottom-up and top down approaches to city benchmark, as well as a novel path toward a people centred smart city benchmarking.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the future of smart city benchmarking will require a shift from the current top-down approach, to a more holistic and bottom-up approach.
, in order to achieve a more effective city benchmarking, a shift of paradigm from "smart city" to "city as a service" is needed.
smart city analytics should be grounded on people perceptions and expectations and, as a result, the concept of smart city should be revised in order to better fit the needs of citizens.
